why: Changing only a presentation field must leave every item id, and therefore every FSRS row, intact across a rebuild. The named falsifier is a ruby re-solve of 今日 orphaning its strength meter and re-showing NEW WORD; the P2 build half of it is a rebuild after a distractor swap that orphans a strength meter.
rule: Hash over prompt, preferred surface, lexeme/concept/grapheme tags and register ONLY (EC-PACK-38). Ruby spans, audio hashes, stroke paths, illustration refs, the accepted-alternate set and the distractor pool are outside the hash.

cases.why: The falsifier proper: the distractor pool is swapped wholesale in a rebuild. A build that hashed the distractors would mint a new id, the learner's FSRS row would stop resolving, and the strength meter would empty on a sentence they have seen for weeks.
EC-PACK-38's own case: a monthly JmdictFurigana release re-solves the ruby spans of 今日.

A reviewer adds an accepted katakana surface to an item with FSRS history. The enumerated answer set IS the tolerance budget (review R24), so it changes often — and it is outside the hash for exactly that reason.
The bake re-renders one clip with a different voice; the audio hash moves.
The exercise moves to another lesson. Position is not identity: a naive index carry-over is what remaps twelve weeks of history onto whatever now occupies slot 413.
The tags arrive in the other order from a re-run tagger. Not a content change.
A SEMANTIC change: the prompt itself. This must mint a new id, or the rule would be 'ids never change', which is a different and useless property.
A semantic change: the preferred surface, which is the FIRST accepted answer. Adding an alternate does not move the id; replacing the preferred one does.
A semantic change: the register. A1 Japanese is masu-form throughout and plain form is an explicit grammar concept, so a register flip is a different item.
A semantic change: a tag. A wrong tag silently corrupts the memory model, which is why the tags are inside the hash and why V4 exists.
